changes.correctAnswer: Proceed with surgery and continue her usual amlodipine
changes.explanation:
BP below 180/110 mm Hg is not a reason to delay elective surgery. She has good functional capacity and no active cardiac condition, so she can proceed on her usual antihypertensive.

Why others are wrong:
• Starting a beta-blocker on the day of surgery increases stroke and death (POISE). The 2024 guideline labels this harmful.
• Rapid IV lowering of asymptomatic BP before induction risks hypotension and has no benefit.
• Stress testing does not help a patient who can do 4 or more METs without symptoms.
• Delaying surgery for stage 2 BP below 180/110 is not recommended.

Takeaway: Do not start a beta-blocker on the day of surgery. Continue chronic BP medications and proceed when BP is below 180/110.

changes.correctAnswer: Postpone the elective surgery and intensify her oral antihypertensive therapy
changes.explanation:
BP of 180/110 or higher with no acute target-organ damage is severe asymptomatic hypertension, not an emergency. For elective major surgery, guidelines support deferring the case and controlling BP with oral therapy over days to weeks.

Why others are wrong:
• IV antihypertensives are for hypertensive emergency (acute organ damage). Here they add risk without benefit.
• An ICU infusion is for hypertensive emergency.
• Sublingual nifedipine causes unpredictable, precipitous BP drops and is not used.
• Proceeding at 188/114 for an elective case ignores the recommendation to defer and optimize.

Takeaway: Severe hypertension without organ damage is treated with oral agents. Elective surgery can wait until BP is controlled.

changes.explanation:
She is normotensive, with no RV strain and a normal troponin, so this is low-risk PE. Anticoagulation alone is the treatment, and a DOAC such as apixaban (10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily) is preferred over warfarin.

• Warfarin alone has no immediate effect and needs overlap with parenteral heparin.

Takeaway: Hemodynamically stable PE without RV strain is treated with anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC. Lytics are not used.

changes.explanation:
A high-bleeding-risk procedure requires interrupting warfarin, usually about 5 days ahead so the INR normalizes. With nonvalvular AF, CHA2DS2-VASc of 3, and no prior stroke or TIA, thrombotic risk is low. The 2017 ACC pathway advises against bridging, which raises bleeding without lowering stroke risk (BRIDGE trial).

Why others are wrong:
• Uninterrupted warfarin is acceptable only for low-bleeding-risk procedures.
• Bridging in low-thrombotic-risk AF increases major bleeding.
• PCC is for urgent reversal or life-threatening bleeding, not planned procedures.
• IV vitamin K is for urgent reversal. Simply holding warfarin is enough for an elective case.

Takeaway: Elective procedure on warfarin for low-risk nonvalvular AF: hold warfarin about 5 days. Do not bridge, and do not use reversal agents.

Hip arthroplasty requires interrupting warfarin. A mechanical mitral valve, especially with AF, carries high thrombotic risk. The 2020 VHD guideline recommends bridging with heparin while the INR is subtherapeutic, then resuming after hemostasis.

Warfarin is the only appropriate anticoagulant for a mechanical valve. With a mechanical AVR plus a thromboembolic risk factor such as AF, the 2020 VHD guideline target INR is 3.0. His INR of 2.8 is in range, so he continues warfarin.

This is an inferior STEMI with right ventricular involvement at a PCI-capable center. Chewed aspirin 162 to 325 mg should be given immediately to every ACS patient without contraindication, while primary PCI proceeds.

changes.correctAnswer: Obtain a 12-lead ECG
changes.explanation:
Suspected ACS requires a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival. The ECG decides between STEMI, which needs reperfusion, and NSTE-ACS, which needs risk stratification. Every other management step depends on it.

Why others are wrong:
• The cath lab is activated based on ECG findings, which are not yet available.
• CT angiography is for suspected dissection or PE, and equal arm BPs make dissection unlikely.
• Anticoagulation follows the ECG-based diagnosis.
• Troponin helps, but the ECG must come first and must not wait on labs.

Takeaway: Get an ECG within 10 minutes in anyone with possible ACS, before any other decision.

changes.explanation:
Prosthetic valves, including transcatheter valves, are among the highest-risk conditions for infective endocarditis. Prophylaxis is reasonable before dental procedures that manipulate gingiva. The regimen is a single dose of amoxicillin 2 g orally 30 to 60 minutes beforehand.

Why others are wrong:
• A prosthetic valve is a high-risk condition that warrants prophylaxis.
• A post-procedure course is not the regimen. Prophylaxis is a single pre-procedure dose.
• The 2021 AHA statement no longer recommends clindamycin, because of C. difficile risk.
• Low-dose aspirin is generally continued for dental extraction.

Takeaway: For prosthetic valves, prior IE, certain CHD, or a cardiac transplant with valvulopathy, give amoxicillin 2 g once before gingival work.

changes.explanation:
This is asymptomatic moderate primary MR (stage B) with normal LV size and function. The 2020 VHD guideline recommends surveillance TTE every 1 to 2 years, so a decline in LV function or progression to severe MR is caught early.

Why others are wrong:

changes.explanation:
This is symptomatic severe AS (stage D1). Aortic valve replacement, surgical or transcatheter as chosen by the heart valve team, is recommended. No medication improves survival, and prognosis without AVR is poor.

Why others are wrong:
• Beta-blockers do not treat AS and can worsen low-output symptoms.
• ACE inhibitors do not relieve fixed outflow obstruction.
• Nitrates can cause severe hypotension in severe AS.
• Surveillance is for asymptomatic disease. Symptoms mean intervention.

changes.explanation:
A child with known asthma who has diffuse bilateral wheeze, prolonged expiration, and rising albuterol use after a viral infection is having an asthma exacerbation, which viral URIs commonly trigger. Treat with short-acting beta-agonist, systemic corticosteroids, and oxygen as needed.

Why others are wrong:
• Pneumonia would cause focal crackles or consolidation, not diffuse wheeze.
• Aspiration causes unilateral or focal findings after a choking episode.
• Bronchiolitis is a diagnosis in children under 2 years.
• Croup causes a barking cough and inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheeze.

Takeaway: Viral-triggered diffuse wheeze in a known asthmatic over age 2 is an asthma exacerbation, not bronchiolitis.

changes.correctAnswer: Sinus tachycardia
changes.explanation:
Upright P waves in I, II, and aVF before every QRS, a normal PR, and a rate of 122 with a clear cause (fever and volume depletion) define sinus tachycardia. Treat the underlying cause with fluids and antipyretics.

Why others are wrong:
• Flutter shows sawtooth waves, usually with a ventricular rate near 150.
• AVNRT is abrupt and usually faster than 150, with P waves hidden or retrograde.
• VT has a wide QRS.
• MAT has 3 or more P-wave morphologies with an irregular rhythm.

Takeaway: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia with normal upright P waves and an obvious trigger is sinus tachycardia. Treat the cause.
